source_title: Reddit is coming for logged-out browsing, and users aren’t having it
source_excerpt:

Reddit plans to shift to a primarily logged-in experience, potentially limiting how people browse the platform without an account.
Nearly 59% of Reddit’s daily active uniques were logged out in Q3 2026, meaning the change could affect the majority of its audience.
Reddit will begin testing the changes in select markets outside the US, but users are already pushing back against the idea.
Reddit’s about to look and feel a lot different, and no, I’m not just talking about the new For You and Following feeds the platform announced yesterday. Reddit is planning something much bigger — something that could fundamentally change how millions access the platform.
Earlier today, Reddit CEO Steve Huffman announced that the platform is transitioning to a primarily logged-in experience, and users are (very) unhappy with the development.
The platform, which launched back in 2005, has always allowed users to browse its content without the need to log in. Of course, those just visiting never really enjoyed the benefits logged-in users did, but they could browse through regardless (barring old.reddit and age-restricted content). Now, Reddit wants to change that.
How do you feel about Reddit moving to a primarily logged-in experience?
Huffman gave some reasons to support the change. He wrote that moving to a logged-in-only experience would improve personalization, encourage more participation, help the company serve more personalized ads, and (most importantly) prevent AI models from scraping content.
In Reddit’s Q3 shareholder letter , Huffman wrote:
According to the company’s Q3 shareholder letter, Reddit averaged 130.3 million daily active uniques in Q3 2026. Out of those, 76.8 million were logged-out visitors, and 53.5 million users were logged in. That essentially means 59% of Reddit’s active user base last quarter accessed the platform without being logged in. In other words, Reddit’s upcoming change could affect the majority of its daily audience, and not just a small subset of users.
Fortunately, it looks like Reddit won’t be locking everything behind a login screen. In a section about boundaries between logged-in and logged-out experiences, Huffman suggested that Reddit’s homepage will remain accessible to all.
Unsurprisingly, the development hasn’t gone down too well with users, and comments under Huffman’s post make that clear. When asked whether this means being constantly blocked by a login prompt when trying to look up a one-off solution, Huffman reiterated that the company will have to test and find the right balance. He added that “the one-off visitor from a shared link or search referred user aren’t the primary target here.”
Others argued that the platform should focus on adding new features and improving existing ones, instead of making the platform less accessible. Some even expressed frustration about the possibility of Reddit becoming like X or Pinterest, where visiting a shared link means being greeted by a login prompt.
Huffman wrote that the company is still trying to figure out the right boundaries, and that it plans to experiment with different approaches in select markets outside the US over the coming months.
